1	\section{Analysis}
2	\label{sec:analysis}
3	
4	The regime-dependent pattern in \S\ref{sec:main-results} establishes \emph{where} SICA succeeds and fails. This section investigates \emph{why}: trace correlation quantifies the SC plateau (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}), symbolic confirmation bias identifies the root cause (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}), process-level independence reveals a deeper bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}), supporting diagnostics confirm the mechanism (\S\ref{sec:diagnostics}), and more than twenty remediation strategies demonstrate a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
5	
6	\subsection{Condorcet Effective-K}
7	\label{sec:effective-k}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:independence} reports Fleiss' $\kappa$ and Effective-K (Eq.~\ref{eq:effk}) across 15 conditions at $K = 12$. Among instruction-tuned models, $\kappa$ ranges from 0.21 to 0.82, yielding $K_{\text{eff}} = 1.20\text{--}3.62$. Qwen3-14B in thinking mode reaches $\kappa = 0.91$ ($K_{\text{eff}} = 1.09$). The four Mistral-7B FOLIO seeds produce $\kappa \in [0.41, 0.51]$ ($K_{\text{eff}} \approx 1.8\text{--}2.2$), yet $\Delta$ ranges from $+3.43$ to $-0.49$\,pp---seed-level constraint quality, not independence, drives the variation. Two conditions are jointly necessary for positive $\Delta$: sufficient $K_{\text{eff}}$ (Qwen conditions with $K_{\text{eff}} \leq 1.30$ never improve) and sufficient SC accuracy (Mistral on ProofWriter with the highest $K_{\text{eff}} = 3.62$ but SC $= 39\%$ produces significant degradation). Even when both hold, sampling variance determines whether the constraint pool is discriminative. Cross-model validation with three families confirms universality: Mistral-7B ($\kappa = 0.44$), LLaMA-3.1-8B ($\kappa = 0.41$), Qwen2.5-7B ($\kappa = 0.66$), and Qwen2.5-14B ($\kappa = 0.74$) all produce $\kappa$ well above zero (Table~\ref{tab:kappa_generalization}; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-kappa}).
10	
11	\begin{table}[t]
12	\centering
13	\small
14	\caption{Trace independence metrics ($K = 12$, sorted by $\kappa$ descending). $\kappa$: Fleiss' Kappa. $K_{\text{eff}}$: Effective-K (Eq.~\ref{eq:effk}). SC: Self-Consistency baseline. $\Delta$: SICA $-$ SC (pp). {*}\,$p < 0.05$; positive $\Delta$ values do not reach significance. multi-T $= T \in \{0.3, 0.7, 1.2\}$, 4 traces each.}
15	\label{tab:independence}
16	\begin{tabular}{@{}llccrr@{}}
17	\toprule
18	Model & Condition & $\kappa$ & $K_{\text{eff}}$ & SC (\%) & $\Delta$ (pp) \\

39	
40	
41	\subsection{Symbolic Confirmation Bias}
42	\label{sec:confirmation-bias}
43	
44	The correlation above manifests through a specific mechanism: self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer regardless of correctness. On Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$), when SICA errs, 83.3\% of extracted constraints support the incorrect majority answer---a bias ratio of $4.97\times$ compared to correct problems. Consequently, 94\% of SICA errors overlap with SC errors: symbolic aggregation adds no independent corrective signal.
45	
46	The 12 instances where SICA corrects SC errors reveal the mechanism's boundary: 43\% of these flips occur when a minority trace provides gold-aligned constraints, suggesting constraint diversity---not MAX-SAT---drives the rare successes. The causal chain is: the model generates an answer, then extracts FOL consistent with that answer; aggregation over such constraints reduces to a weighted majority vote (Eq.~\ref{eq:degenerate}).
47	
48	Iterative refinement does not break this cycle. CEGIS achieves $\Delta = +3.43$\,pp in round~1 but oscillates in rounds~2--5 without convergence, as each step reintroduces model bias. Cross-model extraction (Qwen3-14B or Qwen2.5-14B extracting from Mistral-7B traces) produces accuracy within $\pm 1$\,pp of self-extraction---the bias is a property of LLM formalization itself. The oracle ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}) confirms that 75.9\% of the potential gain is lost to self-extraction quality, localizing confirmation bias as the binding bottleneck.
49	
50	
51	\subsection{Process-Level Independence}
52	\label{sec:process-kappa}
53	
54	Answer-level $\kappa$ may underestimate the independence bottleneck: two traces can follow nearly identical reasoning yet reach different final answers, causing $\kappa$ to treat them as disagreeing. On Mistral-7B FOLIO ($n = 204$), the mean pairwise cosine similarity of chain-of-thought traces (TF-IDF, Eq.~\ref{eq:process-sim}) is $0.69$, far exceeding answer-level $\kappa = 0.41$. These measures are uncorrelated ($r = -0.06$, $p = 0.36$): problems with diverse answers do not exhibit diverse reasoning. We find 9.3\% of trace pairs converge on reasoning ($\cos > 0.8$) while disagreeing on the final answer---apparent answer diversity masking process-level homogeneity.
55	
56	This gap implies that interventions targeting answer diversity (temperature scaling, diverse prompting) may spread answers without altering reasoning paths. Process-level correlation establishes a tighter bound on effective ensemble diversity than answer-level $\kappa$ alone.
57	
58	
59	\subsection{Supporting Diagnostics}
60	\label{sec:diagnostics}
61	
62	Four analyses confirm the mechanism (details in Appendices~\ref{app:extraction}--\ref{app:entropy}). Extraction taxonomy: 91.8\% of constraints are discriminative, but their direction mirrors the majority; 42.9\% are redundant across traces. Constraint ablation ($n = 804$): MAX-SAT and count-only agree on 94.4\% of predictions---the solver adds no value over counting because constraint weights carry information redundant with vote counts. Hyperparameter sensitivity: $K = 12$ is the only setting with $\Delta > 2$\,pp among five values; $T = 0.7$ the only temperature with a positive effect---peaks coincide with low SC baselines. Entropy decomposition: all effects concentrate in high-entropy problems (up to $+12.8$\,pp), but direction depends on accuracy regime.
63	
64	
65	\subsection{Remediation Analysis}
66	\label{sec:remediation}
67	\label{sec:interventions}
68	
69	We test more than twenty remediation strategies spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions. All produce neutral or negative results.
70	
71	\paragraph{Prompt-level interventions.} Nine strategies spanning six dimensions (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:remediation}) all fail. Contrastive prompting reduces non-discriminative constraints from 8.2\% to 6.0\%, but newly discriminative constraints still mirror the majority ($\Delta = -1.1$\,pp). Cross-model extraction fails in both directions: weaker models yield 0\% discriminative constraints; stronger models produce accuracy within $\pm 1$\,pp of self-extraction. Multi-temperature sampling ($T \in \{0.3, 0.7, 1.2\}$) yields $\Delta = 0.00$\,pp.
72	
73	\paragraph{Method-level interventions.} Three strategies target different aspects of the independence bottleneck (Table~\ref{tab:method_interventions}). Independent Constraint Generation (ICG) bypasses trace-constraint coupling by generating constraints directly from premises. Despite producing superior constraints---higher Z3 compilation, lower redundancy---ICG yields $\Delta \approx 0$ across three seeds ($p = .206$, n.s.). Per-constraint-set reranking produces $\kappa = 0.47$, nearly identical to SC's $\kappa = 0.44$: the bottleneck is a property of the model itself. Contrastive scoring yields $\Delta = -9.31$\,pp on FOLIO ($p < 0.01$); 62.7\% of constraints are trivially satisfied. Debate produces $\Delta = -18.63$ and $-23.00$\,pp ($p < 0.001$ on both datasets), with discordant pairs heavily skewed toward correct$\to$wrong flips. 1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Test-time computation scaling through multiple reasoning samples has emerged as a practical alternative to scaling model parameters \citep{snell2025scaling, guo2025deepseekr1}.
4	The dominant aggregation strategy, Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, samples $K$ chain-of-thought traces and selects the majority answer.
5	SC is simple, model-agnostic, and effective---but it is hitting a ceiling.
6	\citet{loo2025reevaluating} demonstrate that gains from increasing $K$ plateau and even decline for strong models.
7	The gap between SC's theoretical promise (independent correct voters converge to truth) and its practical behavior (saturating gains) points to a structural mismatch: same-model traces carry correlated errors, and majority voting has no mechanism to correct shared bias.
8	
9	Confidence-weighted \citep{taubenfeld2025cisc} and universal \citep{chen2024usc} extensions alleviate this to a degree, but the core limitation persists.
10	Recent neuro-symbolic methods---Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm}, LINC \citep{olausson2023linc}, DyLoS \citep{xu2026dylos}, Aristotle \citep{li2025aristotle}, FoVer \citep{wang2025fover}, LogicAgent \citep{luo2025logicagent}---each report gains on logical reasoning, but introduce components beyond the reasoning model: trained verifiers, solver selection, or external knowledge.
11	A simpler question precedes these: can the \emph{same} model that generates reasoning traces also extract useful formal constraints from them?
12	Self-extraction would be a zero-cost upgrade requiring no additional model, training data, or external prover.
13	Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extracted constraints are useful for aggregation.
14	
15	We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}: if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority converges to truth \citep{austensmith1996}.
16	When independence fails \citep{ladha1992correlated}, additional samples carry diminishing information.
17	Measuring inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa}, we find $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across instruction-tuned conditions, yielding Effective-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ for nominal $K = 12$: traces beyond a dozen add negligible independent information (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
18	The bottleneck runs deeper than answer-level agreement suggests.
19	Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), revealing that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on final answers (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
20	When the same model extracts FOL constraints from these correlated traces, the constraints exhibit \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: on problems where the model errs, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
21	Self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires.
22	
23	We study this through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
24	We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 instances with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
25	More than twenty remediation strategies---spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions targeting the independence bottleneck---all produce neutral or negative results, confirming the bottleneck is structural at the 7B--32B scale tested.
26	
27	Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL yields $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
28	The central finding is a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off: Debate reduces $\kappa$ from 0.44 to 0.15 (tripling Eff-$K$) but collapses accuracy by $-18.6$\,pp; SC, Diverse-Prompt, and ICG all cluster at $\kappa \approx 0.40$--$0.47$, forming a same-model ceiling that holds across three model families (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
29	Whether larger models or trained extractors can overcome this remains open.
30	
31	Our contributions are:
32	\begin{enumerate}
33	\item \textbf{Independence-Accuracy Trade-off.} Fleiss' $\kappa$ generalization across four aggregation methods and three model families reveals a Pareto frontier: methods that increase independence destroy accuracy, while methods that preserve accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$). More than twenty remediation strategies all fail (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
34	
35	\item \textbf{Symbolic Confirmation Bias.} Self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer: bias ratio $4.97\times$ on incorrect problems, 94\% error overlap with SC. The causal chain---model generates answer, extracts consistent FOL, Z3 aggregation mirrors majority vote---explains why self-extraction cannot correct errors the model has already committed (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
36	
37	\item \textbf{Process-Level Independence Quantification.} Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), establishing that reasoning processes are more homogeneous than answer distributions suggest. Combined with Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across 15 conditions and three model families, this quantifies the independence ceiling for same-model trace aggregation (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}, \S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
38	
39	\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Pattern and Diagnostics.} Three failure modes---confirmation bias (SC $\geq 60\%$), non-formalizability, error amplification (SC $\leq 40\%$)---create regime boundaries. $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost diagnostic predicting when symbolic augmentation is unlikely to help (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
40	\end{enumerate}

We ground our analysis in the Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785}: if $K$ independent voters each answer correctly with probability $p > 0.5$, the majority converges to truth \citep{austensmith1996}.
When independence fails \citep{ladha1992correlated}, additional samples carry diminishing information.
Measuring inter-trace agreement with Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa}, we find $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across instruction-tuned conditions, yielding Effective-$K = 1.20$--$3.62$ for nominal $K = 12$: traces beyond a dozen add negligible independent information (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}).
The bottleneck runs deeper than answer-level agreement suggests.
Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), revealing that traces share reasoning processes even when they diverge on final answers (\S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).
When the same model extracts FOL constraints from these correlated traces, the constraints exhibit \emph{symbolic confirmation bias}: on problems where the model errs, 83.3\% of self-extracted constraints support the wrong majority answer (bias ratio $4.97\times$), and 94\% of errors overlap with SC (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).
Self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires.

We study this through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA): extract FOL constraints from each of $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicate by syntactic equivalence, and select the answer best supported by a weighted partial MAX-SAT solution via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3} (\S\ref{sec:pipeline}; Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
We evaluate SICA across six models (7B--32B), three reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}), and over 3,000 instances with four-seed replication (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
More than twenty remediation strategies---spanning prompt engineering, method-level redesign, and ten additional directions targeting the independence bottleneck---all produce neutral or negative results, confirming the bottleneck is structural at the 7B--32B scale tested.

Oracle controls confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound: gold FOL yields $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$), yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of this ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
The central finding is a fundamental independence-accuracy trade-off: Debate reduces $\kappa$ from 0.44 to 0.15 (tripling Eff-$K$) but collapses accuracy by $-18.6$\,pp; SC, Diverse-Prompt, and ICG all cluster at $\kappa \approx 0.40$--$0.47$, forming a same-model ceiling that holds across three model families (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).
Whether larger models or trained extractors can overcome this remains open.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Independence-Accuracy Trade-off.} Fleiss' $\kappa$ generalization across four aggregation methods and three model families reveals a Pareto frontier: methods that increase independence destroy accuracy, while methods that preserve accuracy cannot break the correlation floor ($\kappa \geq 0.40$). More than twenty remediation strategies all fail (\S\ref{sec:remediation}).

\item \textbf{Symbolic Confirmation Bias.} Self-extracted constraints systematically confirm the model's majority answer: bias ratio $4.97\times$ on incorrect problems, 94\% error overlap with SC. The causal chain---model generates answer, extracts consistent FOL, Z3 aggregation mirrors majority vote---explains why self-extraction cannot correct errors the model has already committed (\S\ref{sec:confirmation-bias}).

\item \textbf{Process-Level Independence Quantification.} Chain-of-thought cosine similarity ($0.69$) far exceeds answer-level $\kappa$ ($0.41$), establishing that reasoning processes are more homogeneous than answer distributions suggest. Combined with Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$ across 15 conditions and three model families, this quantifies the independence ceiling for same-model trace aggregation (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}, \S\ref{sec:process-kappa}).

\item \textbf{Regime-Dependent Pattern and Diagnostics.} Three failure modes---confirmation bias (SC $\geq 60\%$), non-formalizability, error amplification (SC $\leq 40\%$)---create regime boundaries. $C_0$ (multi-candidate rate) combined with SC accuracy provides a zero-cost diagnostic predicting when symbolic augmentation is unlikely to help (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
\end{enumerate}
